area: Area VII. Emergencies and Accident Reporting
objective: By the end of this lesson you can apply the 14 CFR 91.207 ELT rules (exceptions, batteries, inspection), test an ELT and handle a false alarm the way the AIM asks, and plan a flight plan, survival gear and on-the-ground actions so you are found quickly after an off-airport landing.
why: An off-airport landing that everyone walks away from can still end badly if nobody knows where you are. The AIM is blunt: without a flight plan, about 36 hours normally pass before family concern starts an alert, and an injured survivor's life expectancy drops sharply in the first 24 hours. The ELT, the flight plan and the kit you pack are what close that gap.

prereading.what: The ELT rule: who needs one, where it is mounted, batteries, the 12-month inspection, ferry flights and exceptions.
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.207

prereading.what: How 121.5 and 406 MHz ELTs are detected, how to test one, false alarms, and what to report if you hear one in flight.
prereading.label: AIM 6-2-4

prereading.what: Search and rescue: who does it, why a filed flight plan matters, VFR SAR protection, survival equipment and body signals.
prereading.label: AIM 6-2-6

prereading.what: Filing and activating a VFR flight plan, assumed departure times and noting a GPS tracking service.
prereading.label: AIM 5-1-5

prereading.what: Item 19 of the flight plan: the supplemental information kept for search and rescue.
prereading.label: AIM Appendix 4-20 to 4-21

prereading.what: Extra radio and ELT actions when a crash landing or ditching is coming, and why you stay with the airplane.
prereading.label: AIM 6-3-2

prereading.what: What 12 calendar months means, and the ELT inspection and battery rules in plain words.
prereading.label: PHAK 9-8 to 9-9

warmup: Think first: today is October 24. You rent a club airplane for a three-hour trip over mountains and forest. The ELT inspection sticker reads September 10 of last year, and the battery date is two years away. The ELT is an older 121.5 MHz unit. Is the airplane legal for this flight? If you went down with no flight plan, who would notice, and when? Write your answers, then check them at the end of chunks 2 and 5.

key_terms.def: A small, self-contained radio transmitter that automatically sends an emergency signal on 121.5, 243.0 or 406.0 MHz on crash impact.
Total transmit time added up across every activation, real or accidental. More than 1 cumulative hour of use means a new (or recharged) battery.

Per the PHAK (written for the annual inspection), a period that runs from any day of a month to the last day of the same month the following year. 91.207(d) uses the same words for the ELT inspection.
A digital ELT that satellites detect. It can carry the owner's contact information, and newer models the aircraft's position. It must be registered with NOAA.
An older analog ELT with a downward swept tone. Satellites stopped listening for it in 2009, so only nearby ATC or an overflying aircraft may hear it.
The international satellite distress alerting system that detects activated 406 MHz beacons. NOAA runs the U.S. part.
A Coast Guard or Air Force center that directs search and rescue in its region and receives 406 MHz alert data.
What you get by filing and activating a VFR flight plan: if you do not close it, a search starts about half an hour after your ETA.
Supplemental information on the flight plan form (endurance, persons on board, pilot contact, aircraft color, survival gear). Kept by the filing service for search and rescue, not sent to ATC.
A portable 406 MHz beacon a person carries. The AIM suggests that pilots who do not own the airplane check its ELT and, as appropriate, get one.
Large symbols survivors lay out on the ground for search pilots, such as V for require assistance and X for require medical assistance.
An ELT that starts transmitting without a crash, for example after a hard landing or when the airplane is moved. It looks exactly like a real distress signal.

chunks.title: The rule: which airplanes need an ELT

body.p: An ELT is a small, self-contained radio transmitter that automatically sends an emergency signal on 121.5, 243.0 or 406.0 MHz upon crash impact [[24:378|AFH G-6]]. The AIM says ELTs are required for most general aviation airplanes [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a1]].

callout.text: For Part 91 flights, there must be attached to the airplane an approved personal type or an approved automatic type ELT that is in operable condition [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)(2)]]. Certain Part 121 and 125 operations and all Part 135 operations need the automatic type [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)(1)]].

bullets: After June 21, 1995, an ELT that meets TSO-C91 may not be used for new installations [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]].
The ELT must be attached so that crash damage to it is unlikely. Fixed and deployable automatic types go as far aft as practicable [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(b)]].
The VFR day equipment list includes an ELT, if required by 91.207 [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(15)]].

head: 91.207(f) exceptions that can matter to a light single
Source
rows: Training operations conducted entirely within a 50 NM radius of the airport where the local flight operations began
Aircraft equipped to carry not more than one person
Design and testing; new aircraft being made, prepared and delivered; agricultural application; research and development
Showing compliance with regulations, crew training, exhibition, air racing or market surveys

ELT temporarily removed for inspection, repair, modification or replacement: a records entry (date removed, make, model, serial number, reason), an "ELT not installed" placard in view of the pilot, and no flight more than 90 days after it was first removed

body.p: Two ferry cases are allowed without a working ELT: flying a newly acquired airplane to where an ELT will be installed, and flying an airplane with an inoperative ELT from a place where repairs cannot be made to a place where they can. Only required crewmembers may be aboard [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(e)]].

callout.text: Interpretation: the 50 NM exception is for training operations [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(3)]]. A sightseeing hop or a lunch run 20 NM from home is not training, so the ELT rule applies in full.

The AIM suggests that pilots who do not own the airplane check its ELT and, as appropriate, get a 406 MHz personal locator beacon [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4a2(g)]]. Interpretation: 91.207 requires the ELT to be attached to the airplane [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]], so a beacon in your pocket is an extra, not the required ELT. The sources say nothing more about it.

check.q: An owner flies alone in his four-seat airplane on a local sightseeing flight. The ELT is inoperative but still installed. Does the single-occupant exception help him?
check.a: No. The exception covers aircraft equipped to carry not more than one person, not flights with one person aboard [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(9)]]. It is not a training flight either [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(3)]].

head: Replace (or recharge) ELT batteries when
Source
rows: The transmitter has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour
50 percent of their useful life (or of their useful life of charge) has expired, as set by the transmitter manufacturer
Exception: the 50 percent rule does not apply to batteries, such as water-activated batteries, that are essentially unaffected during probable storage intervals

body.p: The new expiration date must be legibly marked on the outside of the transmitter and entered in the aircraft maintenance record [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

callout.text: Each required ELT must be inspected within 12 calendar months after the last inspection for: proper installation, battery corrosion, operation of the controls and crash sensor, and the presence of a sufficient signal radiated from its antenna [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]] [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

body.p: The PHAK explains that a period of 12 calendar months runs from any day of a month to the last day of the same month the following year [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. It says this about the annual inspection; interpretation: 91.207(d) uses the same words, so read it the same way.

The AFH says the pilot should check the logbooks or a summary of the airworthy status before flight, and its list of required items includes the ELT inspection and the ELT battery due date [[24:39|AFH 2-2]] [[24:40|AFH 2-3]]. The flight review guide in AC 61-98E lists the ELT rule under both required equipment and inspections [[15:40|AC 61-98E App E]].

callout.text: Note: that AFH list says "within the last 12 months" [[24:40|AFH 2-3]]. The rule says within 12 calendar months after the last inspection [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]. Use the CFR wording.

body.p: If you fly outside the United States, the PHAK says the owner or operator needs a current FCC radio station license for the aircraft radios, including the ELT [[1:243|PHAK 9-13]].

check.q: Warm-up answer, part 1: the ELT was last inspected September 10 of last year and today is October 24. Legal?
check.a: No. More than 13 months have passed, so the ELT was not inspected within 12 calendar months after the last inspection [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]. On the PHAK reading of calendar months it ran out at the end of September [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. The battery date is fine, but both must be met.

chunks.title: 121.5 or 406: how the signal gets you found

body.p: ELTs transmit on 121.5, 243.0 or 406 MHz. The 121.5 and 243.0 MHz units are analog. The 406 MHz unit is digital and can be encoded with the owner's contact information or aircraft data; the latest models can also send the aircraft's position, and 406 MHz units transmit a stronger signal [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2]].

callout.text: Changed: as of 2009, the Cospas-Sarsat satellites stopped monitoring 121.5 and 243.0 MHz. An airplane with only an analog ELT depends on a nearby ATC facility receiving the signal, or on an overflying aircraft hearing it and telling ATC [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(b)]].

head: 406 MHz ELT
121.5 MHz ELT
rows: A nearby ATC facility or an aircraft overhead [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(b)]]
NOAA sends the alert to an Air Force or Coast Guard RCC, which can phone the owner to check [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(c)]]
SAR normally waits for confirmation, such as an overdue aircraft; this can take hours [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4a2(g)]]
Digital; can carry owner or aircraft data, and on the latest models position. Also has a low-power 121.5 MHz homing transmitter for the final search phase [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(c)]]
Analog; a distinctive downward swept tone on 121.5 and 243.0 MHz [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(d)]]

bullets: The FCC requires 406 MHz ELTs to be registered with NOAA, and the FAA's TSO-C126 requires it too. NOAA keeps the U.S. registration database and runs the U.S. part of Cospas-Sarsat [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(a)]].

If it is armed and feels crash forces, an ELT is designed to activate and transmit continuously for at least 48 hours over a wide temperature range. It helps only if it survives the crash and is activated [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(e)]].
Because of the satellites, a 406 MHz alert also narrows the search to a smaller area than a 121.5 MHz alert [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(c)]].
NOAA and the FAA highly encourage owners to switch to a 406 MHz ELT [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4a2(g)]].

callout.text: Application: the RCC's phone call goes to the owner information on file with NOAA [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(c)]]. If that information is out of date, the quick check that can cancel a needless search cannot happen. The sources do not say how to update it.

check.q: A 121.5-only ELT goes off after a crash in a remote valley. No flight plan was filed. Who is likely to hear it?
check.a: Not the satellites, which stopped listening in 2009. Only a nearby ATC facility or an aircraft flying over that monitors 121.5 [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(b)]], and SAR normally waits for confirmation such as an overdue report [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4a2(g)]].

chunks.title: Testing an ELT, and handling a false alarm

bullets: Test ELTs by the manufacturer's instructions, preferably in a shielded or screened room or a special test container, so no false alert goes out [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4b]].

When that cannot be done, analog 121.5/243 MHz ELTs should be tested only during the first 5 minutes after any hour. Outside that window, coordinate with the nearest FAA control tower. Keep it to three audible sweeps, and use a dummy load if the antenna is removable [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4b]].
Test digital 406 MHz ELTs only by the unit manufacturer's instructions [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4b]].
Airborne tests are not authorized [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4b]].

callout.text: An accidental activation sends a signal that cannot be told apart from a real one. It leads to expensive searches, can block a real distress signal, and frequent false alarms breed complacency [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4c]].

body.p: Inadvertent activations have come from aerobatics, hard landings, ground crews moving the airplane, and maintenance [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4c]]. Catch them by listening on 121.5 (and 243.0) MHz:

head: Monitor 121.5 MHz
Source
rows: In flight, when a receiver is available
Before engine shutdown at the end of each flight
When the ELT is handled during installation or maintenance, or maintenance is done near it
When a ground crew moves the aircraft

body.p: If you hear an ELT signal, turn off your own ELT to see whether it was the one transmitting. If it was activated, maintenance might be needed before it goes back to ARMED, and you should notify the nearest air traffic facility of the inadvertent activation [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4c]].

callout.text: Every minute counts toward the battery rule: replace or recharge the battery when the transmitter has been in use for more than 1 cumulative hour [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)(1)]]. Interpretation: the rule counts time "in use" and makes no exception, so read it to include accidental run time and tests.

body.p: If you hear a signal in flight, report to the nearest air traffic facility your position when you first heard it, when you last heard it, and at maximum signal strength, plus your altitudes and the frequency. Give positions relative to a navaid if possible, and a bearing if you have homing equipment [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4d]] [[34:32|AIM 6-2-4d]].

check.q: A mechanic must ground test an analog ELT in the airplane and can remove its antenna. What does the AIM say to put in its place?
check.a: A dummy load, so the test signal is not broadcast [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4b]].

chunks.title: The flight plan: your search and rescue protection

body.p: Search and rescue (SAR) is a lifesaving service of the federal agencies in the National SAR Plan and the states. Resources include the Coast Guard, DoD, the Civil Air Patrol, the Coast Guard Auxiliary, law enforcement and volunteers [[34:32|AIM 6-2-6a]]. The Coast Guard coordinates SAR in the Maritime Region and the Air Force in the Inland Region, through Rescue Coordination Centers. Aircraft emergency information normally reaches an RCC through an ARTCC or FSS [[34:33|AIM 6-2-6b]].

callout.text: Within the continental U.S., a VFR flight plan is not normally required [[33:331|AIM 5-1-5a1]]. DVFR flight plans are required for VFR flights into an ADIZ, and a VFR flight to an international destination needs a filed and activated flight plan [[33:331|AIM 5-1-5a2]] [[33:331|AIM 5-1-5a4]]. Once a flight plan is activated, the PIC must notify an FAA Flight Service Station or ATC facility when canceling or completing the flight [[60:464|14 CFR 91.153(b)]].

body.p: A filed flight plan is the most timely and effective sign that an aircraft is overdue [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f1(b)]]. The AIM calls filing one "an excellent low-cost insurance policy" [[33:324|AIM 5-1-2]].

head: VFR SAR protection (AIM 6-2-6g)
Source
rows: File only to the first point of intended landing and refile for each leg. With one long plan, nobody may start looking until 30 minutes after your ETA at the final destination
Land somewhere other than your destination: report it to the nearest FSS and give your original destination
Delayed more than 30 minutes at an en route stop: report it to the nearest FSS
ETE changes by 30 minutes or more: report a new ETA. Fail to respond within half an hour after your ETA and a search starts
Close the plan immediately after arrival. The pilot is responsible; it is not closed automatically
Stay on your planned course: an accurate position speeds rescue

bullets: You must activate the plan with Flight Service. Control towers do not automatically activate VFR flight plans [[33:331|AIM 5-1-5a]] [[33:332|AIM 5-1-5f]].
VFR proposals are normally kept for two hours after the proposed departure time [[33:331|AIM 5-1-5d]].
With an assumed departure time, the plan goes active at that time. If you do not update it, SAR will be based on the assumed time [[33:331|AIM 5-1-5e]].

Item 19 (endurance, persons on board, pilot name and contact, aircraft color, at minimum) is kept by the filing service for SAR, not sent to ATC. For VFR plans it goes as a separate message to the destination FSS [[34:289|AIM Appendix 4-20]].
In Item 19 N/ remarks, note survival equipment, any personal GPS locating service, and a responsible party who can confirm your arrival [[34:290|AIM Appendix 4-21]] [[33:332|AIM 5-1-5j]].

callout.text: Even on a local flight, tell someone at the departure point where you are going and your route if it is not direct [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f2]].

check.q: Warm-up answer, part 2: with no flight plan, who notices you are missing, and when?
check.a: Possibly no one for a long time. An Air Force review found that without a flight plan, 36 hours normally pass before family concern starts an alert [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f4]]. A filed plan starts a search half an hour after your ETA [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g4]].

chunks.title: Survival equipment: what is required, and what is wise

body.p: For flight over uninhabited land, the AIM says it is wise to take survival equipment for the climate and terrain and to know how to use it. After a forced landing at sea, survival depends on crew proficiency in emergency procedures and on water survival equipment [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6h]]. The PHAK asks, for trips over remote areas, whether suitable clothing, water and survival gear are aboard [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]], and the AIH personal minimums checklist lists survival gear appropriate for the flight and terrain [[25:207|AIH D-2]].

head: Item
Part 91 rule for a piston single?
Source
rows: Approved flotation gear for each occupant, plus at least one pyrotechnic signaling device
Only when operated for hire over water and beyond power-off gliding distance from shore
No, unless it is a fractional ownership program aircraft under subpart K. Subpart F covers large airplanes, turbojet-powered multiengine airplanes and those fractional aircraft
Survival kit for flight over land
Interpretation: no Part 91 rule found in these sources; the AIM recommends it

callout.text: Seaplane note: in its seaplane safety paragraph, written for seaplanes flying over or into remote areas, the AIM says minimum survival kits are recommended for summer and winter and are required by law for flight into sparsely settled areas of Canada and Alaska, and that Alaska DOT and Canadian Ministry of Transport officials can give the specific requirements. It advises one container that is easy to reach and preferably floats [[34:165|AIM 7-6-9d]] [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9d]]. The sources give no landplane version of this line.

body.p: Over water, intact wings and fuel tanks of a well-ditched airplane usually float it for at least several minutes [[24:356|AFH 18-7]]. The AIM's seaplane section adds that FAA-approved life vests are inflated only after you exit the airplane, and that passengers must be briefed on where they are and how to use them [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9e]].

bullets: The PHAK SAFETY passenger briefing includes the emergency or survival kit: where it is and what is in it [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].
Pilots and passengers should know how to activate the ELT if manual activation is needed, and how to verify it is transmitting after a crash or manual activation [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(f)]].

callout.text: Application: pack for the night on the ground, not for the flight. Ask what you would need to spend a night next to the airplane in that terrain and season. The sources leave the exact list to you.

check.q: You fly your own single, with no pay involved, 40 NM offshore to an island. Does Part 91 require life vests?
check.a: Not by these rules. 91.205(b)(12) applies to for-hire flights [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]], and 91.509 applies only to the airplanes listed in 91.501, such as large and turbojet-powered multiengine airplanes [[60:527|14 CFR 91.501]]. But the AIM says survival at sea depends on water survival equipment [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6h]].

chunks.title: When an off-airport landing is coming

body.p: The AFH separates a forced landing (immediate, because flight cannot continue) from a precautionary landing (planned, when flight is possible but inadvisable). It warns that too many precautionary landings become forced landings because of wishful thinking [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].
The distress call itself is taught in RF.VII.A. When a crash landing or ditching is imminent, the AIM adds these actions to help SAR [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2c]]:

bullets: Time permitting, add ELT status, visible landmarks, aircraft color, number of persons on board and emergency equipment on board [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2c]].
Actuate your ELT if the installation permits [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2c]].
For a crash landing or ditching, if fire risk is not a consideration, set your radio for continuous transmission [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2c]].
If you must ditch, try to ditch near a surface vessel. An FAA facility may be able to get the nearest vessel's position from a Coast Guard RCC [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2c]].

callout.text: Turning off the electrical system before touchdown reduces the chance of a post-crash fire, but the AFH says not to turn the battery master off until you no longer need electrical power for vital systems [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Interpretation: make the call and switch on the ELT first. The ELT is battery operated [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2]].

check.q: Your ELT has a remote switch on the panel. A crash landing is coming. What does the AIM say to do with it?
check.a: Actuate the ELT if the installation permits, and give its status in your transmission [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2c]].

chunks.title: On the ground: stay, signal, survive

callout.text: After a crash landing, unless you have good reason to believe search aircraft or ground teams will not find you, it is best to stay with the aircraft and prepare ways to signal search aircraft [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2c5]].

bullets: Check that the ELT is working and transmitting [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(f)]]. Application: a radio tuned to 121.5 MHz is one way to hear it.

Time matters. The National SAR Plan says an injured survivor's life expectancy decreases as much as 80 percent during the first 24 hours, and uninjured survivors' chances drop rapidly after the first 3 days [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f3]].
If you made a precautionary landing at an airport or field and the airplane is fine, report the landing to the nearest FSS with your original destination [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g2]].

body.p: Lay out ground symbols with fabric, wood, stones or anything available, with as much color contrast as possible. Make them at least 10 feet high, exactly as shown. Also use radio, flares, smoke or other means. On snow, drag, shovel or tramp the symbols; the depressions look black from the air. A pilot acknowledges by rocking the wings [[34:36|AIM FIG 6-2-1]].

Body signals let you talk to a pilot circling overhead. Stand in the open against a background that is not confusing, move slowly, and repeat each signal until you are sure the pilot understands [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6i]].

head: Body signal
Meaning
Source
rows: Need medical assistance, urgent. Used only when life is at stake
Can proceed shortly, wait if practicable
Need mechanical help or parts, long delay
Both arms waved across the face
Do not attempt to land here
Squat, both arms forward, point the landing direction
Aircraft dips its nose several times

callout.text: If you are the one who spots a downed aircraft: a yellow cross means it was already reported. Otherwise note type, number and signs of survivors, fix the position from a navaid, transmit it to the nearest FAA or other radio facility, orbit if you can, and make a full report after landing [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6j]].

check.q: How large should ground-air symbols be?
check.a: At least 10 feet high, laid out exactly as shown [[34:36|AIM FIG 6-2-1]].

chunks.title: Risk: remote terrain with no flight plan and no gear

body.p: The AIM says search efforts are often wasted and rescue delayed because pilots take off without telling anyone where they are going [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f2]]. The PHAK and AIH both ask, before a trip over remote areas, whether clothing, water and survival gear are aboard [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]] [[25:10|AIH 1-6]].

head: What pilots say
What the sources say
rows: True within the continental U.S. [[33:331|AIM 5-1-5]], but a filed plan is the most timely and effective sign that you are overdue [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f1(b)]]

Radar facilities treat loss of radar and radio without a termination notice as a possible emergency, and SAR may start [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f1(a)]]. The AIM still says to file a flight plan for your safety [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f2]]
Only if it survives the crash and is activated [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(e)]]. A 121.5-only alert may wait hours for confirmation [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4a2(g)]]
"I'll file one plan for the whole trip."
A mishap on the first leg may not be searched for until 30 minutes after your final ETA [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g1]]
The gear is for the time on the ground: injured survivors lose as much as 80 percent of life expectancy in the first 24 hours [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f3]]

callout.text: Application: before a remote flight, pick the worst stretch of the route and ask: if the engine quits here, who knows where I am, how soon will they look, and what will we have for the first night? If any answer is weak, fix it on the ground.

check.q: Without a flight plan, how long does the AIM say normally passes before family concern starts an alert?
check.a: About 36 hours, from an Air Force review of 325 SAR missions [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f4]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: plan survival gear and SAR protection

body.p: **Use the same list before every flight over remote terrain or water.**

bullets: 1. ELT: attached and operable, inspected within 12 calendar months, battery date not passed, and less than 1 cumulative hour of use [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]] [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]] [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]].
2. Know the ELT type. If it is 121.5 only, think about a 406 MHz personal locator beacon [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4a2(g)]].
3. Know how to switch the ELT on by hand and check that it is transmitting, and brief passengers on it and on the survival kit [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(f)]] [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

4. Pack survival equipment for the climate and terrain, and water survival gear over water [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6h]]. For hire beyond gliding distance from shore: flotation gear and a pyrotechnic signal are required [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]].
5. File a VFR flight plan to the first landing and refile each leg. Fill Item 19, and note a GPS tracker in N/ remarks [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g1]] [[34:289|AIM Appendix 4-20]] [[34:290|AIM Appendix 4-21]].
6. Activate the plan with Flight Service; the tower will not [[33:331|AIM 5-1-5]].
7. En route: report a new ETA if the ETE changes by 30 minutes or more, a stop delay over 30 minutes, or a landing somewhere else [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g]].
8. Close the plan right after arrival [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g5]], and listen on 121.5 MHz before shutdown [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4c]].

check.q: You land at the second stop of a three-leg trip and have lunch. What must happen before leg 3?
check.a: Close the leg 2 plan, which is your job [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g5]] [[60:464|14 CFR 91.153(b)]], then file and activate a plan for leg 3 [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g1]] [[33:331|AIM 5-1-5]].

head: Error
Fix
rows: Counting a PLB in your pocket as the required ELT
Interpretation: 91.207 requires an approved ELT attached to the airplane [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]]
Thinking the 50 NM exception covers any flight near home
It covers training operations only [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(3)]]
Reading the inspection as "the last 12 months"
Within 12 calendar months after the last inspection [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]] [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]
More than 1 cumulative hour of use means a new battery [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)(1)]]. Interpretation: accidental run time counts as use
Testing an ELT in flight, or an analog unit at any time of the hour
Airborne tests are not authorized; analog ground tests only in the first 5 minutes after the hour, or coordinate with the tower [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4b]]
Expecting the tower to open your VFR flight plan
A search starts if you do not respond within half an hour after your ETA [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g4]]
Walking away from the airplane after a crash landing
Stay with it unless you have good reason to think you will not be found [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2c5]]

check.q: A passenger asks why you are showing her the ELT switch. What does the AIM say?
check.a: Pilots and passengers should know how to activate the ELT if manual activation is needed and how to verify it is transmitting [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(f)]].

Sections list Airplane Documents (airworthiness certificate, registration, radio station license, operating limitations, weight and balance), Airplane Inspections with due dates (annual, 100 hour, VOR, altimeter, static system and encoder), and a Required Equipment column for VFR day that includes an ELT line.

f2.alt: A table of five messages and code symbols: 1 Require assistance, V; 2 Require medical assistance, X; 3 No or Negative, N; 4 Yes or Affirmative, Y; 5 Proceeding in this direction, an arrow. Below: If in doubt, use international symbol SOS, and six layout instructions, including symbols at least 10 feet high and pilots acknowledging by rocking wings.

f3.caption: AIM FIG 6-2-3, Urgent Medical Assistance, and FIG 6-2-4, All OK (AIM 6-2-9).
f3.alt: Left: a person lying flat on the ground with arms stretched out, labeled Need medical assistance, urgent, used only when life is at stake. Right: a standing person with one arm raised straight overhead, labeled All OK, do not wait, wave one arm overhead.

Right: a person in a squat with both arms straight forward, labeled Land here, both arms forward horizontally, squatting and point in direction of landing, repeat.

scenario.title: A fall trip over the backcountry in a club 182
scenario.setup: You and two friends plan a late October trip in a club Cessna 182: about 200 NM over mountains and national forest to a lodge airport, with one fuel stop on the way. The club airplane has an older 121.5 MHz ELT. The forecast is VFR, but nights are near freezing and much of the route is far from roads.

questions.q: Before you go, what ELT items do you check, and where?
questions.a: That an approved ELT is attached and operable [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]]; that it was inspected within 12 calendar months after the last inspection [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]] [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]; and the battery replacement date, marked on the outside of the transmitter and in the maintenance record [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]]. The AFH list of records to check before flight includes both [[24:40|AFH 2-3]].

questions.q: What does the 121.5-only ELT change about how you would be found, and what could you add?
questions.a: Satellites stopped monitoring 121.5 MHz in 2009, so only nearby ATC or an overflying aircraft may hear it [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(b)]], and SAR normally waits for confirmation such as an overdue report, which can take hours. The AIM suggests non-owner pilots get a 406 MHz personal locator beacon [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4a2(g)]].

questions.q: How do you file to get the best SAR protection?
questions.a: File a VFR flight plan only to the fuel stop, then refile for the second leg [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g1]]. Activate each one with Flight Service [[33:331|AIM 5-1-5]]. Fill in Item 19 (endurance, persons on board, pilot contact, aircraft color) and note any GPS tracker and your survival equipment in N/ remarks [[34:289|AIM Appendix 4-20]] [[34:290|AIM Appendix 4-21]].

questions.q: What survival gear does Part 91 require for this flight, and what do you take?
questions.a: Interpretation: no Part 91 rule in these sources requires a survival kit for a private flight over land; flotation gear is required only for hire over water beyond gliding distance [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(b)(12)]]. The AIM says to take equipment for the climate and terrain and know how to use it [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6h]], and the PHAK names clothing, water and survival gear for remote areas [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]. Brief its location and contents with the SAFETY briefing [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

questions.q: At the fuel stop, before shutdown, you hear a swept tone on 121.5 MHz. What do you do?
questions.a: Turn off your ELT to see if it was the one transmitting. If it was, maintenance might be needed before it goes back to ARMED, and you notify the nearest air traffic facility [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4c]]. Interpretation: count the run time toward the 1 cumulative hour battery limit [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)(1)]].

questions.q: On leg 2, low clouds force you to land at another airport 40 NM short. What now?
questions.a: Report the landing to the nearest FSS and give your original destination [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g2]], and make sure the plan is closed, which is your responsibility [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g5]] [[60:464|14 CFR 91.153(b)]]. Otherwise a search starts half an hour after your ETA [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g4]].

skills.do: Given a planned flight (route, terrain, water, season, airplane and its ELT), say whether the ELT meets 91.207 and any exception, choose the survival equipment the flight needs and which items Part 91 actually requires, and set up SAR protection: how to file, activate, update and close the flight plan, what goes in Item 19, and what you and your passengers would do after an off-airport landing.
skills.practice: Before your next cross-country, open the maintenance records with an instructor and find the ELT inspection and battery entries [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]] [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]. Locate the ELT and its switch, and listen on 121.5 MHz before shutdown [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4c]]. Then plan one remote trip on paper: file leg-by-leg flight plans with Item 19 filled in [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g1]] [[34:289|AIM Appendix 4-20]], write a packing list for that terrain and season [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6h]], and practice the ground-air code and body signals with your passengers [[34:36|AIM FIG 6-2-1]] [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6i]].

quiz.q: For a Part 91 flight in a four-seat single, what ELT does 91.207 require?
options: An automatic type ELT only
None, if the flight stays in the United States
Any 406 MHz beacon carried by the pilot
An approved personal type or automatic type ELT attached to the airplane and in operable condition
quiz.why: For operations other than those in 91.207(a)(1), an approved personal type or automatic type ELT in operable condition must be attached to the airplane [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]].

quiz.q: Which statement about TSO-C91 ELTs is correct?
options: After June 21, 1995 they may not be used for new installations
They are required in all new airplanes
They must be replaced by every annual inspection
They are the only type approved for Part 135
quiz.why: After June 21, 1995, an ELT that meets TSO-C91 may not be used for new installations [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]].

quiz.q: Which ELT batteries are exempt from the 50 percent useful life replacement rule?
options: Batteries, such as water-activated ones, that are essentially unaffected during probable storage intervals
Batteries less than 2 years old
Rechargeable batteries
None are exempt
quiz.why: Paragraph (c)(2) does not apply to batteries such as water-activated batteries that are essentially unaffected during storage [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

quiz.q: How do U.S. SAR forces usually treat a first 121.5 MHz ELT alert compared with a 406 MHz alert?
options: Exactly the same
They ignore 121.5 alerts completely
They respond faster, because 121.5 is louder
They wait for confirmation, such as an overdue aircraft, which can take hours
quiz.why: Because of false alerts and no registration database, SAR normally waits for confirmation for 121.5/243.0 alerts, while 406 MHz alerts get a response in minutes [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4a2(g)]].

quiz.q: What must the 12-calendar-month ELT inspection in 91.207(d) look at?
options: Only the battery replacement date
A three-sweep test in flight with tower approval
Proper installation, battery corrosion, operation of the controls and crash sensor, and a sufficient signal radiated from the antenna
The NOAA registration and the FCC station license
quiz.why: 91.207(d) lists proper installation, battery corrosion, operation of the controls and crash sensor, and the presence of a sufficient signal radiated from its antenna [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]. Airborne tests are not authorized [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4b]].

quiz.q: In flight you hear an ELT signal on 121.5 MHz. Which report does the AIM ask you to give the nearest air traffic facility?
options: Only your call sign
Nothing; ATC hears it already
The ELT's registration number
Your position when first heard, when last heard, and at maximum strength, plus altitudes and frequency
quiz.why: Report positions when the signal was first heard, last heard and at maximum strength, and your altitudes and the frequency [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4d]] [[34:32|AIM 6-2-4d]].

quiz.q: Under the National Search and Rescue Plan, who coordinates SAR in the Inland Region?
options: The U.S. Air Force
The U.S. Coast Guard
The FAA
NOAA
quiz.why: The Coast Guard coordinates SAR in the Maritime Region and the USAF in the Inland Region [[34:33|AIM 6-2-6b]].

quiz.q: Who closes an activated VFR flight plan?
options: The destination tower, automatically
It closes itself at the ETA
The FBO at the destination
The pilot in command, by notifying an FSS or ATC facility
quiz.why: The PIC notifies an FSS or ATC facility on canceling or completing the flight [[60:464|14 CFR 91.153(b)]]; plans are not closed automatically [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g5]].

quiz.q: A search pilot circling overhead sees your ground symbol. How will the pilot acknowledge it?
options: By flashing the landing light
By rocking the wings from side to side
By dropping a message
By climbing straight up
quiz.why: The FIG 6-2-1 instructions say the pilot acknowledges by rocking the wings from side to side [[34:36|AIM FIG 6-2-1]].

final_quiz.q: Your ELT failed at a remote strip with no repair shop. You may ferry the airplane to a shop. A friend wants to ride along. What does 91.207 say?
options: Fine, if the friend is a pilot
Only required crewmembers may be carried
Fine, if you file a flight plan
Fine, if you stay within 50 NM
final_quiz.why: No person other than required crewmembers may be carried on a 91.207(e) ferry flight [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(e)]].

final_quiz.q: The club's four-seat airplane has an inoperative ELT that has not been removed. A member wants to fly a solo lunch trip to an airport 30 NM away. Does an exception apply?
options: Yes, the 50 NM exception
Yes, if the trip is under one hour
Yes, because only one person is aboard
No. The 50 NM exception is for training operations, and none of the other exceptions fit
final_quiz.why: The 50 NM exception covers training operations [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(3)]]; the one-person exception is for aircraft equipped to carry not more than one person [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(9)]]. Interpretation: a lunch trip is neither.

final_quiz.q: After an off-airport landing in brown, dry grassland, you gather material for a ground-air symbol. Which choice does the AIM advise?
options: Material that blends with the ground so it looks tidy from the air
Material with as much color contrast as possible against the background
Only white material, whatever the background
Small symbols close to the airplane so the wreck and the symbol are seen together
final_quiz.why: Provide as much color contrast as possible between the material and the background, and make symbols at least 10 feet high [[34:36|AIM FIG 6-2-1]].

final_quiz.q: A registered 406 MHz ELT activates while the airplane sits locked in its hangar. What does the AIM say can happen next?
options: A full search starts with no checks
Nothing, because satellites ignore hangars
The RCC can phone the owner to verify, and a costly search is avoided; the owner can deactivate the ELT
The FAA suspends the registration
final_quiz.why: With a registered 406 MHz ELT, the RCC can contact the owner to verify the aircraft's status; if it is safely in a hangar, a costly search is avoided, and the owner can deactivate the ELT [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(c)]].

final_quiz.q: You plan four legs with three stops. Which filing gives the best VFR SAR protection?
options: One plan to the final destination with the stops in remarks
No plan, with flight following on every leg
One plan with an assumed departure time
A separate plan to each stop, refiled for each leg
final_quiz.why: For maximum protection, file only to the first point of intended landing and refile for each leg; otherwise no one may look until 30 minutes after the final ETA [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g1]].

final_quiz.q: Weather forces you to land at an airport 50 NM short of your destination. Your plan is still open. What does the AIM ask you to do?
options: Nothing until the ETA passes
Call the destination tower only
Report the landing to the nearest FSS and give your original destination
Refile a new plan and leave the old one open
final_quiz.why: If you land somewhere other than the intended destination, report the landing to the nearest FAA FSS and advise them of your original destination [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g2]].

final_quiz.q: A rescue airplane circles while you stand under trees at the edge of a clearing, quickly flashing body signals. What does the AIM advise?
options: Stay in the shade and signal faster so the pilot sees more
Stand in the open, against a background that is not confusing, move slowly and repeat each signal until sure the pilot understands
Give each signal once only, so the pilot is not confused
Save body signals for night, when the pilot can see them better
final_quiz.why: Stand in the open, make sure the background seen from the air is not confusing, go through the motions slowly and repeat each signal until you are positive the pilot understands [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6i]].

final_quiz.q: You are down in deep snow with no fabric or wood. How can you make a ground-air symbol?
options: You cannot; snow hides everything
Drag, shovel or tramp the snow; the depressions appear black from the air
Write it in small letters near the airplane
Only use the radio
final_quiz.why: On snow-covered ground, signals can be made by dragging, shoveling or tramping; depressed areas appear black from the air [[34:36|AIM FIG 6-2-1]].

final_quiz.q: On an activated VFR flight plan, you think about leaving your filed route to cut across a remote ridge area and save 15 minutes. What does the AIM say that bears on this?
options: Nothing; the ELT gives searchers your exact position
Search aircraft fly only along airways
Rescue speed depends on how accurately your position can be found; following the plan on course speeds rescue
Leaving the route cancels the flight plan automatically
final_quiz.why: The rapidity of rescue depends on how accurately your position can be determined; if the flight plan has been followed and you are on course, rescue will be expedited [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g6]].

final_quiz.q: Flying over a canyon, you spot a wrecked airplane with a large yellow cross on it. What does that tell you?
options: Survivors need medical help
Do not land here
The crash has already been reported and identified
The occupants walked out to the north
final_quiz.why: A yellow cross means the crash has already been reported and identified [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6j]].

final_quiz.q: You plan a VFR flight from Vermont to an airport in Canada. What does AIM 5-1-5 say about a flight plan?
options: A filed and activated flight plan is required
None is needed if you use flight following
It is recommended but not required
Only an IFR flight plan is accepted
final_quiz.why: VFR flight to an international destination requires a filed and activated flight plan [[33:331|AIM 5-1-5a4]].

final_quiz.q: You use a commercial GPS tracking service. Where does the AIM encourage you to note it when filing?
options: Item 19 N/ remarks
Item 7, aircraft identification
Item 10, equipment
Nowhere; ATC does not need it
final_quiz.why: Pilots using commercial GPS tracking services are encouraged to note the service in Item 19 N/ (survival equipment remarks) [[33:332|AIM 5-1-5j]] [[34:290|AIM Appendix 4-21]].

final_quiz.q: You file with an assumed departure time of 0900, then leave at 0950 without updating it. What does the AIM warn?
options: The plan is canceled automatically
The tower will correct it
SAR activities will be based on the assumed departure time
Nothing; ETAs are recalculated by radar
final_quiz.why: If an assumed departure time is not updated, search and rescue activities will be based on it; revising it is the pilot's responsibility [[33:331|AIM 5-1-5e]].

takeaways: A Part 91 airplane needs an approved ELT attached and operable unless a 91.207(f) exception applies; the 50 NM exception is for training only.
Replace the ELT battery after more than 1 cumulative hour of use or at 50 percent of its useful life; inspect the ELT within 12 calendar months.
Satellites hear only 406 MHz ELTs. A 121.5 MHz alert may wait hours, so consider a 406 MHz PLB.
Test only on the ground, as the AIM allows, and listen on 121.5 MHz before every shutdown; report an accidental activation.
File a VFR flight plan to each landing, activate it with Flight Service, update it, and close it yourself.
Take survival gear for the climate and terrain, brief it, and know how to switch on the ELT.
After an off-airport landing, stay with the airplane, check the ELT, and signal with ground symbols and body signals.
cfi_notes: The AFH list of records to check before flight says ELT inspection "within the last 12 months" [[24:40|AFH 2-3]]. 91.207(d) says within 12 calendar months after the last inspection [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]. Teach the CFR and the PHAK meaning of calendar months [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]].

The AFH glossary lists 121.5, 243.0 and 406.0 MHz without saying satellites stopped monitoring the analog frequencies in 2009 [[24:378|AFH G-6]] [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(b)]]. Teach the AIM picture of detection and response time.

Interpretation: the sources do not say whether a personal locator beacon satisfies 91.207. The rule requires an approved ELT attached to the airplane [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]], so teach a PLB as an addition the AIM recommends [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4a2(g)]], not a substitute.

The AIM testing guidance uses "should" and "not authorized" [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4b]]; 91.207 itself sets only the inspection, not a test schedule [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]. Present the AIM items as FAA guidance.

The AIM's line about survival kits required by law in Canada and Alaska sits in its seaplane safety paragraph [[34:165|AIM 7-6-9d]]. Present it as a seaplane note; the sources give no landplane list, so send pilots to those authorities.

AIM 6-2-6g still speaks of filing with an FAA FSS [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g1]], while AIM 5-1-2 and 5-1-5 allow websites and apps to file and activate [[33:324|AIM 5-1-2]] [[33:331|AIM 5-1-5]]. What matters is that the plan is activated and closed.
Keep the boundaries with the other Area VII lessons: the distress call and ATC services are RF.VII.A, and NTSB notice of an overdue aircraft believed in an accident is RF.VII.B.
The AIM quotes the 80 percent and 36 hour figures without dates [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f3]] [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f4]]. Use them to show why time matters, not as precise current statistics.

On the ramp, have the pilot find the ELT, its remote switch and the battery date label, then listen on 121.5 MHz at shutdown [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4c]] [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]]. Most renters have never looked.
gaps: The useful life of a given ELT battery and the manufacturer's test procedure come from the ELT maker; the sources do not give them.
How to register or update a 406 MHz ELT or PLB with NOAA, and what the registration must contain, is not in the sources.
The sources give no packing list for a survival kit, and no Alaska or Canadian legal kit lists; the AIM points to those officials [[34:166|AIM 7-6-9d]].
The meaning of each letter in the Item 19 S/, J/ and R/ boxes is not on the AIM pages read; the AIM only says to cross out items not carried [[34:290|AIM Appendix 4-21]].
Who may perform the 12-month ELT inspection, and whether it is usually done with the annual, is not stated in these sources.

activities.title: Who does what when an ELT goes off
activities.intro: Tap a name, then the job it does.

pairs.r: Keeps the U.S. 406 MHz registration database
Requires 406 MHz ELTs to be registered with NOAA
The FAA 406 MHz ELT standard, which also requires registration
Satellites that detect an activated 406 MHz beacon
Can phone the owner to check the airplane's status
Alerts the SAR system about an aircraft in difficulty, overdue or missing
One of the operational resources that carry out SAR

activities.why: NOAA, FCC, TSO-C126, Cospas-Sarsat and the RCC call [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(a)]] [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(c)]]; ARTCCs and FSSs alert SAR [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f]]; operational resources [[34:32|AIM 6-2-6a]].

activities.title: You spot a downed airplane
activities.intro: Flying over the hills, you see a wreck below. Use the arrows to put the AIM steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Look for a yellow cross on the wreck
If you can, note the aircraft type and number and any sign of survivors
Fix the crash position from a navaid and describe the area for ground parties
Transmit the information to the nearest FAA or other radio facility
If you can, orbit the scene to guide other units in until relieved
After landing, make a complete report to the nearest FAA facility or an Air Force or Coast Guard RCC
activities.why: AIM 6-2-6j lists these steps in this numbered order, 1 to 6 [[34:35|AIM 6-2-6j]].

activities.title: True or false: flight plans and SAR
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Part 91 requires a VFR flight plan for every cross-country flight within the continental U.S.
cards.why: False. Within the continental U.S. a VFR flight plan is not normally required [[33:331|AIM 5-1-5a1]].

cards.s: A control tower automatically activates your VFR flight plan when you take off.
cards.why: False. Pilots activate with Flight Service; towers do not automatically activate VFR plans [[33:331|AIM 5-1-5a]] [[33:332|AIM 5-1-5f]].

cards.s: A filed flight plan is the most timely and effective indicator that an aircraft is overdue.
VFR flights into an Air Defense Identification Zone (ADIZ), other than DoD and law enforcement flights, must file a DVFR flight plan.
VFR flight plan proposals are normally kept for two hours after the proposed departure time.
Item 19 supplemental information is transmitted to ATC as part of the flight plan.
cards.why: False. It is kept by the filing service for SAR and not sent to ATC [[34:289|AIM Appendix 4-20]].

activities.title: Required, excepted, or just wise?
activities.intro: Each case is a Part 91 flight in a piston single unless it says otherwise. Tap a case, then where it belongs.
buckets: Not required: an exception or the rule's scope leaves it out
Not required, but FAA guidance recommends it

items.t: An ELT for a private pilot's 200 NM trip to visit family in a four-seat airplane
An ELT for a 30-minute sightseeing hop that stays within 20 NM of home
An ELT on a local dual lesson that stays within 30 NM of the departure airport
An ELT on a flight ferrying a newly bought airplane, crew only, to the shop that will install its ELT
Liferafts on a private flight 120 NM over water in a piston single you own outright
A VFR flight plan for a domestic cross-country
A 406 MHz PLB when the rental has a 121.5-only ELT
Telling someone at the departure point your destination and route

activities.why: ELT required unless an exception applies [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(a)]]; sightseeing is not a training operation [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(3)]]. Exceptions: training within 50 NM [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)(3)]] and the ferry of a newly acquired airplane [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(e)(1)]]. 91.509 liferafts apply only to the airplanes in 91.501 (large, turbojet multiengine, fractional program) [[60:527|14 CFR 91.501]] [[60:530|14 CFR 91.509]]. Recommended: flight plan [[33:331|AIM 5-1-5a1]], PLB [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4a2(g)]], telling someone [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f2]].

activities.title: Read the ground-air code
activities.intro: The message column is blank. Drag each message to its code symbol.
activities.why: V require assistance, X require medical assistance, N no, Y yes, arrow proceeding in this direction [[34:36|AIM FIG 6-2-1]].

activities.title: Minutes and hours that decide a search
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: You go down 30 minutes before your ETA on an activated VFR flight plan and cannot call anyone. Without a plan, the AIM says about 36 hours normally pass before family concern starts an alert. About how many hours sooner does the flight plan get a search started?
items.why: With the plan: 30 minutes to the ETA plus about 30 minutes after it = 1 hour after the mishap [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g4]]. Without: about 36 hours [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6f4]]. 36 - 1 = 35 hours.

items.q: Item 19 E/ asks for fuel endurance in hours and minutes. Your airplane has 53 gallons usable and burns 12 gallons per hour. What is the endurance in minutes?
items.why: 53 / 12 = 4.417 hours; 4.417 x 60 = 265 minutes, entered as 4 hours 25 minutes [[34:290|AIM Appendix 4-21]]. Application: endurance is usable fuel divided by burn rate.

items.q: You file one plan for a trip with stops: departure 0800, ETE to the final destination 5 hours 20 minutes. You go down on the first leg at 0850 and cannot call anyone. How many minutes after the mishap would a search normally start?
items.why: ETA 0800 + 5:20 = 1320. Search about 30 minutes later, 1350 [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g1]]. 1350 - 0850 = 5 hours = 300 minutes.

items.q: Same mishap, but you had filed only to the first stop with an ETE of 1 hour 20 minutes. How many minutes after the mishap would a search normally start?
Your filed ETE was 2 hours 5 minutes. Headwinds make the new ETE 2 hours 40 minutes. By how many minutes did the ETE change?
items.why: 160 - 125 = 35 minutes. That is 30 minutes or more, so report a new ETA to the nearest FSS [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g4]].

activities.title: Three friends, one 182, and the backcountry
activities.intro: You and two friends fly a club Cessna 182 in late October over mountains and national forest to a lodge airport, with one fuel stop. A friend files one VFR flight plan through to the lodge, with a 30-minute stop on the way.

steps.s: Your friend asks what must go in Item 19 at a minimum for this domestic flight.
options: Nothing; Item 19 is only for international flights
Endurance, persons on board, pilot name and contact information, and aircraft color
Only the survival equipment boxes
The route and cruising altitude
steps.why: Minimum required Item 19 entries for a domestic flight are endurance, persons on board, pilot name and contact information, and color of aircraft [[34:289|AIM Appendix 4-20]].

steps.s: At the fuel stop the fuel truck is slow. You will leave about 50 minutes later than planned, and the plan to the lodge is still open.
options: Nothing; the plan already covers the stop
Close the plan and fly leg 2 without one
Report the delay to the nearest FSS and give your original destination
Ask the tower to change your ETA
steps.why: If you land en route and are delayed more than 30 minutes, report it to the nearest FSS and give your original destination [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6g3]]. Towers do not routinely handle VFR flight plans [[33:332|AIM 5-1-5f]].

steps.s: On leg 2 the engine runs rough over forest, and you land hard in a logging clearing. Nobody is badly hurt at first, but you cannot tell whether the ELT went off.
options: Leave it; an ELT always activates in a crash
Turn it off to save the battery for later
Switch it on by hand if needed and check that it is transmitting
Leave it alone until a search airplane shows up
steps.why: Pilots and passengers should know how to activate the ELT by hand and verify it is transmitting after a crash [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(f)]]; it helps only if it survives and is activated [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4a2(e)]].

steps.s: By morning one friend is weak and confused from a head injury. A search airplane circles overhead. Which body signal asks for urgent medical help?
options: Lie down with arms stretched out
Wave one arm overhead
Hold both arms out horizontally
Cup your hands over your ears
steps.why: Lying down with arms out means need medical assistance, urgent, used only when life is at stake [[34:37|AIM FIG 6-2-3]]. One arm overhead is all OK, do not wait [[34:37|AIM FIG 6-2-4]]; both arms horizontal is long delay [[34:38|AIM FIG 6-2-6]]; cupped hands over ears is our receiver is operating [[34:39|AIM FIG 6-2-8]].

steps.s: You squat, point both arms at the clearing and make the land here signal. The pilot fishtails the airplane. What is the reply?
options: Affirmative (yes)
Drop message
Message received and understood
Negative (no)
steps.why: Fishtailing is the negative reply from an aircraft [[34:43|AIM FIG 6-2-15]]. Dipping the nose is affirmative [[34:42|AIM FIG 6-2-14]], and rocking the wings by day means message received and understood [[34:43|AIM FIG 6-2-16]]. Land here signal [[34:40|AIM FIG 6-2-10]].
